opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it should reason the way we'd want any rational agent to reason under uncertainty: it should be choosing actions that maximize expected utility, given what it believes about the world and what it's actually trying to achieve. But the interesting part is in the details of both of those pieces.

On the belief side, the car never really knows the state of the world. It doesn't know exactly where that pedestrian is going to step, whether the car in the next lane is about to merge, whether there's a child behind that parked van. So it has to maintain a belief state, a probability distribution over what might be going on, and crucially it has to reason about how its own actions will change what it gets to observe. Sometimes the right action is to slow down or nudge forward precisely because it'll give you more information. A lot of the early systems treated perception as a separate front end that hands over "the answer," and then planning works on that as if it were certain. That's a mistake, and you see it in the failures.

On the objective side, I'd say this is where people tend to be too glib. It's tempting to write down a cost function: so many points for getting there quickly, a big penalty for a collision, something for passenger comfort. But we don't actually know how to specify those tradeoffs correctly, and if you optimize a misspecified objective hard enough you get behavior nobody wanted. The car should, to some degree, be uncertain about what the right tradeoffs are and defer to human norms and human preferences, including the preferences of the other people on the road, not just the passenger. Driving is fundamentally a social activity. You're constantly predicting what other drivers intend and signaling your own intentions, and they're doing the same with you. So the reasoning has to be game-theoretic in a sense, or at least it has to model other agents as agents rather than as moving obstacles.

And then there's the computational reality: you can't solve that full problem exactly in real time. So you need good approximations, hierarchical planning, abstractions that let you think at the level of "change lanes" or "yield at this intersection" rather than steering angles, and you need to be thoughtful about where you spend computation. That, to me, is the real research challenge: building systems that are principled about uncertainty and about objectives, but still tractable enough to drive a car at sixty miles an hour.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the question itself contains a bit of a trap. People often imagine that the system should be sitting there, at a given moment, choosing among discrete actions: brake, swerve, continue. But that's really not how it should be thinking at all, if "thinking" is the right word.

The right framework, and this goes back to what I'd call the standard model of AI, is decision-theoretic. You have uncertainty about the state of the world. You have uncertainty about how other agents, pedestrians, cyclists, other drivers, are going to behave. And you have some objective. The rational action is the one that maximizes expected utility over the possible futures, taking all of that uncertainty into account. So it's not "which action do I take now," it's "which policy, which way of behaving over the next several seconds, leads to the best distribution of outcomes."

Now, the second thing I'd want to say is about that objective, because this is where I think people have been getting it wrong, not just in driving but across AI generally. The naive approach is to write down a fixed objective: get to the destination quickly, don't collide with things, obey the traffic laws, weight these somehow, and optimize. The problem is that we're not actually capable of writing down the objective correctly. You will always leave something out. You might weight comfort against time in a way that turns out to be aggressive in ways the passengers find terrifying. You might not have anticipated the situation where the road is blocked by a fallen tree and the only way forward is to cross a solid line. If the system is certain about its objective and optimizes it, it will do things we don't want.

So what I've been arguing is that the system should be uncertain about what humans actually want. It should treat the objective as something to be learned from human behavior and human feedback, not something handed to it as a fixed specification. And an interesting consequence of that uncertainty is that the system becomes more deferential. If it's unsure whether a passenger would rather arrive thirty seconds later or experience a hard braking maneuver, it has an incentive to behave conservatively, to ask, or to pay attention to what the passenger does. A system that is certain about its objective has no reason to let a human override it. A system that is uncertain does.

And then there's the question of the other agents on the road. A lot of the public discussion gets dragged into these trolley problem scenarios, and I think that's largely a distraction. Those situations, where you have certainty that one of two bad outcomes will occur and you must choose, almost never arise. What does arise, constantly, is the need to predict and negotiate with other humans. Are they going to yield? Do they see me? If I nudge forward, will they understand that as a signal? That's a game-theoretic problem, and humans do it with remarkable subtlety. The autonomous system needs some model of the other participants as agents with their own goals and beliefs, not just as moving obstacles with predictable trajectories.

So to put it together: reason under uncertainty about the world, maintain uncertainty about the objective itself and learn it from people, and treat the other road users as agents rather than physics. If you get those three things right, a lot of the dramatic dilemmas people worry about simply don't come up, because the system behaves cautiously enough that it rarely finds itself in them.

astra-6.text:
Well, it has to reason about the consequences of its actions under uncertainty. It doesn’t know exactly what the pedestrian is going to do, or whether the driver in the next lane has seen it. So it needs to consider possible outcomes, their probabilities, and how desirable or undesirable they are, and choose an action accordingly.

But there’s a further uncertainty that I think is very important: what exactly should it be optimizing? We might say, “Get me to the airport quickly,” but that doesn’t mean we’re willing to accept any amount of risk to save a minute. The system shouldn’t take a stated objective as a complete specification of what we care about. It should remain uncertain about our preferences, with strong reasons to behave cautiously where a mistake could cause serious harm.

And, of course, it has to take account of everyone affected by its actions, not just the passenger. Driving is a particularly clear example of why an intelligent machine needs more than the ability to achieve a goal. It needs to understand that the goal we give it is only a partial description of what we actually want.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it has to reason about the possible consequences of its actions, and those consequences depend on what other road users are going to do. If I start moving into this lane, will the other driver slow down, or will they keep coming? So it’s making decisions under uncertainty, including uncertainty about the intentions of other people.

But there’s also uncertainty about what we want. We don’t simply want it to get to the destination as quickly as possible, because that might involve unacceptable risks. Nor do we want it to eliminate all risk, because then it would probably never leave the driveway. It has to make trade-offs among safety, progress, comfort, and so on, in a way that reflects human preferences. And it shouldn’t assume that some particular numerical trade-off we’ve written down is necessarily the right one.
